3. The defendant having entered appearance filed written statement contending inter alia that the suit is barred by limitation etc. and further stated that the plaintiff sent 2000 gunny bags of paddy which were of very inferior quality and the paddy was mixed with unwanted materials and the said paddy supplied to the defendant by the plaintiff was kept in the open air as a result the defendant raised protest to the plaintiff in that regard and in reply the plaintiff agreed to accept less quantity of rice proportionate to the damage as aforesaid and the defendants supplied the rice to the plaintiff on different dates but at one stage due to onslaught of flood and natural calamities the rice mill of the defendant suffered severe damages, despite such a position the defendant when informed the plaintiff about the same, he demanded undue advantage in favour of the plaintiff which when turned down by the defendant; the plaintiff then brought G.R Case No.204 of 1982 under section 406 of the Penal code against the defendant and in that case the defendant having been put to trial, were acquitted of the charge by a judgment dated 04.05.1985; thereafter having suppressed the outcome of G.R Case No.204 of 1982 the plaintiff has brought the instant suit which is liable to be dismissed. 

 4. The suit was taken up for hearing eventually upon framing 6(six) issues including one on the question of limitation and at the hearing the plaintiff examined one witness in support of their case while the defendant also examined one to bring home their case narrated in the written statement thereafter having heard both sides and upon consideration of the materials placed before him the learned Joint District Judge decreed the suit with the claim of an amount of taka 16,14,241.00 in favour of the plaintiff by his judgment and decree dated June 15,2004 passed in Money Suit No.18 of 1990. 

 6. Mr. Shorful Islam Khan, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr. Mamun Chowdhury, has taken as through the materials on record including the impugned judgment and decree by pointing out the sole point of limitation and submits to the effect that the instant suit is hopelessly barred by limitation and that admitting the position as aforesaid the plaintiff while instituting the suit filed an application for condonation of delay ( albeit wrongly ) and on receipt of the plaint the learned Joint District Judge by order No.1 dated 14.11.1990 registered the suit along with an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act containing a prayer made by the plaintiff seeking condonation of delay in filing the suit and on receipt of the said application, 03.01.1991 was fixed by the learned Joint District Judge for hearing of the said application for condonation, meanwhile summons were also issued upon the defendants but on a perusal of the order sheet it appears that the said application under section 5 of the limitation Act filed by the plaintiff was not disposed of either way on any subsequent date till the suit was disposed of although an issue was framed as to whether the suit is barred by limitation and in dealing the said issue the learned Joint District Judge, answered the issue in the language as under:- 

 7. Referring to the said position Mr. Shoriful Islam Khan submits that Section 5 of the Limitation act has got no manner of application in bringing a suit beyond time although the plaintiff in the instant suit had filed an application for the purpose which ought to have been held by the learned Joint District Judge as a misconceived one. 

 8. Referring to the provision of Section 3 of the Limitation Act Mr. Khan submits that "every suit if instituted after the prescribed period of limitation shall be dismissed although limitation has not been set up as a defence" is peremptory, and it is the duty of the court to notice of the Limitation Act and give effect to it even though it is not referred to in the pleadings. 

 9. In substantiating his submission the learned Advocate for the appellant placed reliance in the case of Mokbul Ahmed Vs. Oskar Pratap Narain Singh reported in 37 Bombay Law Report (PC) 533. The learned Advocate for the appellant also submits that the onus is upon the plaintiff initially to show that his suit was not instituted after the period prescribed by schedule one and accordingly is not required to be dismissed under section 3 of the Limitation Act. 

 11. The learned Advocate for the appellant also placed reliance in this connection to the case of Shafiq Ahmed Vs. Mirza Muhammad Anwar Beg reported in 20 DLR (WP)113. Mr. Khan submits further that in the instant case the learned Joint District Judge has referred to a notice dated 15.06.1990 allegedly issued by the plaintiff to the defendant to save the limitation involved in the suit although as a matter of fact Section 19 of the Limitation Act envisages acknowledgement to take effect for fresh computation of the period of limitation must be proved to be of a time before expiration of the period prescribed for an action and secondly, must be in writing and lastly be signed by the person against whom the right is claimed. 

 14. We have heard the learned Advocates from both sides perused the materials on record including the decisions cited from both sides wherefrom it transpires that the impugned judgment and decree has been challenged by the appellant on the sole point of limitation, therefore, the result of this appeal hinges on one single question as to whether the suit was in fact barred by limitation or otherwise and having concentrated our attention to the said question of limitation we find that the suit was registered on the basis of a plaint on 14.11.90 and in presenting the plaint the plaintiff opted for filing a separate application under Sections 5 of the Limitation Act praying for condonation of delay in filing the suit. On receipt of the said application the trial court fixed a date for disposal thereof fixing 03.10.1991 but on that date the application was not disposed of either way. On a close scrutiny of the order sheet we do not find any order on subsequent date till the disposal of the suit, disposing of the application for condonation of delay although the said application was a misconceived one. But it was incumbent upon the learned Joint District Judge to dispose of the same but it was not done unfortunately. Subsequently it appears when the issues were framed specific issue was drawn to the effect as to whether the suit was barred by limitations and the said issue involved in the suit has been disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge in the manner as we have already quoted in the forgoing paragraph, therefore, it is evident that the trial court laid emphasis on the positions that the defendant did not press the said issue before him and in doing so it is apparent that the learned Joint District Judge did not apply his judicial mind to the language expressed in the provision of Section 3 of the Limitation Act which we feel it proper to quote in this connection. Section 3 of the Limitation Act reads as under 

 "Dismissal of the suits, ETC, instituted. ETC, after period of limitation-Subject to the provisions of contained in section 4 to 25 (inclusive) every suit instituted, appeal preferred, and application made, after the period of limitation prescribed therefore by the first schedule shall be dismissed although limitation has not been set up as a defence. 

 15. On a plain reading of the expression made in the aforesaid provision of law, it is apparent that very suit must be entertained within the period of limitation prescribed therefor by the 1st schedule of the Limitation Act. Article 115 prescribed a period of three years "when the contract is broken, or (where there are successive breaches) when the breach in respect of which the suit is instituted occurs or (where the breach is continuing) when it ceases'. But in the instant case we find that the plaintiff himself was hesitant whether the suit was in time or not therefore application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act was filed by him before the trial court for registration of the suit. In this connection the first case referred to by the learned Advocate for the appellant in the case of Mokbul Ahmed Vs. Onkar Pratap Narain Singh. Having gone through the said decision of the Privy Council we find, in that case their lordships while interpreting section 3 of the Indian Limitation Act, held in the language as under :- 

 "every suit or case instituted after the period of limitation prescribed therefor by the first schedule shall be dismissed, although limitation has not be set up as a defence, is peremptory and it is the duty of the court to notice the Indian Limitation Act and give effect to it, even though it is not referred to in the pleadings. 

 17. Therefore, we have no hesitation to hold further that a suit which is beyond time as per the first schedule of the Limitation Act prescribing certain period of time, is a mandatory provision and no amount of discretion can excuse, such a mandate beyond the said period because of the position as has been held by their lordships in the Privy Council that this discretion is a statutory discretion and not a general discretion. Statutory discretion in other words a discretion which can neither be expended nor be reduced at the exercise thereof by the court, unlike the general discretion where the same can be exercised with reference to the exigencies involved in that particular case but it is otherwise in respect of statutory discretion. 

 18. Therefore, we are in respectful agreement with theft lordships of the Judicial Committee in holding that there is difference between a statutory discretion and a general discretion and section 3 provides specific period for doing certain act in the first schedule of the Limitation Act is undoubtedly a statutory discretion not a general one, therefore, mandatory. 

 19. The second decision referred to by the learned Advocate for the appellant is the case of Sir Muhammad Akbar Khan Vs. Mst. Moti and others reported in PLD 1947 PC 322. Having gone through the said decision we find that in that case their lordships have interpreted section 3 of the Limitation Act from a different angle of vision and in doing so, it was opined. that the burden rests in the first instance upon the plaintiff to show that his suit was not instituted after the period prescribed therefor by Schedule 1 of the Limitation Act and accordingly is not required to be dismissed under section 3, from such observation as available in the judgment delivered by the Judicial Committee in the said case it appears that not only the suit be dismissed even if the plea is not taken by the defendant in a suit on the point of limitation which is filed beyond the prescribed period but also it is incumbent upon the plaintiff to prove first that his suit is not beyond the period prescribed by the law of Limitation particularly section 3 and the requirement of to schedule of the Limitation Act and in the instant case before as we find that the trial court laid emphasis on an alleged notice demanding repayment of the amount treating the same as acknowledgement under section 19 of the Limitation Act. 

 20. Turning to the other judgments referred from our own jurisdiction in the case of Saroj Kanto Sarker being dead his legal representatives Asit Sarker and others Vs. Seraj ud Dowla and others reported in 56 DLR39. The other decision reported in 20 DLR (W.P) 113 and ongoing through the sane we find that the decision in respect of section 3 of the Limitation Act, has been taken in the same line as that of the one we have reproduced from the two decisions of the Privy Council, where a Division Bench of the Lahore High Court held the Court should, in fact, proceed under section 3 of the Limitation Act which provides that if a suit is brought after the period of Limitation prescribed thereof, the Court is bound to dismiss it Although the defendant does not raise the objection of limitation. 

 21. In view of the position as above, we find that the instant suit was, as a matter of fact a suit barred by section 3 read with Article 115 of the Limitation Act, 1908. 

 22. While disposing of the question of Limitation, in the impugned judgment, as we have already quoted in the forgoing paragraphs, it appears that the learned Joint District Judge, heavily relied on the claim of the plaintiff that he issued a notice on 15.03.1990 upon the defendant raising a claim for the payment thereof and presumably with reference to section 19 of the Limitation Act, the trial court maintained the suit treating the said notice as one of acknowledgement as contemplated under section 19 of the Limitation Act. We feel it proper to quote the provision of law as embodied in section 19 of the Limitation Act for proper understanding which reads as under:- 

 (1) Where, before the expiration of the period prescribed for a suit or application in respect of any property or right, an acknowledgment of liability in respect of such property or right has been made in writing signed by the party against whom such property or right is claimed or by some person through whom he derives title or liability a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the acknowledgement was so signed. 

 23. On a plain reading of the said provision of law we find that the legislators contemplated three fold requirements for the purpose of treating an action into acknowledgement under section 19 of the Limitation Act, and these are the acknowledgement must be taken effect for computing of a fresh period before expiration of the period prescribed for the same, secondly, the acknowledgement must be in writing and thirdly and lastly the acknowledgement is signed by the person against whom the right is claimed, in our considered opinion, we are in respectful agreement with the judgment delivered by Mr. Md. Abdur Rashid, J. in the case of Saroj Kanto Sarker Vs. Serajud-Dowla and others reported in 56 DLR 39 which has rightly been pointed out by the learned Advocate for the appellant. 

 24. Turing to the facts involved in the instant suit we find that the plaintiff's claim that the notice was served upon the defendant raising the claim in the suit, the plaint is silent as to whether this notice issued upon the defendant was directed initially for the purpose of suit or not as a matter of fact, it was not. Secondly the acknowledge was also not in writing and the same was not received by the proper person in the instant case, therefore, the question of acknowledgement by signing does not arise in the instant case. In our opinion, the trial court wrongly relied section 19 of the Limitation Act in entertaining the instant suit. 

 25. As to the submission made by the learned Deputy Attorney General in this appeal we find that he has also referred to a decision in the case of Ittyavira Mathai Vs.Varkey Varkey and others reported in AIR 1964 (SC) 907 to substantiate his submission to the effect that question of limitation raised before the Supreme Court being not one purely on law but mixed question of fact and law this plea in the specific form was not raised by the defendant either in the written statement or in the appeal before the High Court Division and specific ground was not taken even in the petition for grant of certificate, the suit is barred by time and the Supreme Court refused leave to raise the point before them. 

 26. Having gone through the said judgment we find that this decision was taken by the Supreme Court of India in a case where the court having jurisdiction over the subject matter of the suit or over the part thereto, though bound to decide right may decide wrong; and that even though it decides wrong it would not be doing something having had no jurisdiction to do. It had the jurisdiction over the subject matter and it had the jurisdiction over the party and, therefore merely because it made an error in deciding a vital issue in the suit it cannot be said that it has acted beyond its jurisdiction. Courts have jurisdiction to decide right or to decide wrong and even though they decide wrong the decrees rendered by them cannot be treated as nullities. Such a principle set out by the Indian Supreme court in a subsequent suit where the previous decree was challenged on the question of limitation, and the learned Judges of the Supreme Court decided in the way as disclosed above lint in the instant case before us we are on the self some appeal arising out of the self some judgment and the appeal is a continuation of the suit, therefore the decision cited by the learned Deputy Attorney General is discernible as such not applicable. 

 27. In view what has been stated above we find substance in this appeal, particularly in view of the fact that we are of considered opinion that the instant suit is hopelessly barred by limitation, therefore, the decree passed therein is bound to be set aside. Therefore, the appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment and decree dated 15.06.2004 passed by the Joint District Judge,1st Court, Naogoan in Money Suit No.18 of 1990 is hereby set aside.
